wiki.tagline: Turn a codebase you don't know into a clear, readable wiki.
wiki.when: You've joined a new repo, you're documenting a project, or you want teammates to onboard by reading instead of asking around.
example: Open the repo you want documented, load this kit, and start a new chat.
Say: "Onboard this codebase and write a wiki to docs/."
codebase-onboarding maps the tech stack, the entry points, and the folder structure.
repo-scan inventories the files, and code-tour walks you through the important paths.
architecture and architecture-decision-records capture how it's built and why those choices were made.
documentation and docs-page turn all of that into linked Markdown pages; knowledge-ops keeps them organized.
You end up with a docs/ wiki a new teammate can read start to finish.
tips: Load the kit, then start a fresh chat so the skills come online.
Point Bob at the actual repo folder before you ask.
Ask for it 'written to docs/' so you get real files, not just a chat answer.

product-frameworks.tagline: The three PM thinking frameworks most tools skip: why users come (Jobs to Be Done), why they stay (Hook Model), and why they convert (CRO).
product-frameworks.when: Retention or growth is the problem — people try the product but don't stick, or don't convert — and you want discovery rooted in real motivation, not feature requests.
example: Start with jobs-to-be-done: run switch interviews to find the real job and, crucially, the ANXIETY blocking the switch.
Use opportunity-solution-tree to map that job to a few solution bets instead of jumping to features.
Apply hook-model to design the return loop: internal trigger -> easy action -> variable reward -> investment. Run the ethics gate before shipping.
At first-use or the paywall, use cro-objections: list the 5 doubts a real visitor has and answer each with evidence, in their own words.
Prove it with cohort-analysis: does the retention curve flatten? That's the number that says the loop works.
value-proposition and north-star-metric keep the story and the one metric honest throughout.
tips: Write the job solution-free (verb + object + context) before proposing anything.
Design the INTERNAL trigger first — an external notification alone never forms a habit.
In cro-objections, use the customer's exact words; matching their language is what converts.
Pick ONE north-star (return rate, not signups) so retention work has a scoreboard.

pm-methodology.tagline: Take a product idea from a blank page to shipped, measured, and iterated — one anchor skill per phase.
pm-methodology.when: You want a repeatable process instead of ad-hoc PM work, or you are onboarding to a structured product lifecycle.
example: Foundation: foundation-lean-canvas — capture the bet on one page (problem, users, value, the one metric).
Discover: discover-interview-synthesis — turn raw interviews into patterns and real needs.
Define: define-jtbd-canvas — frame the job the product is hired to do.
Develop: develop-solution-brief — shape the solution and its rationale before building.
Deliver: deliver-prd — write the PRD and hand off to build.
Measure: measure-experiment-design — design the experiment that tells you if it worked.
Iterate: iterate-retrospective — capture what you learned and decide the next move.
tips: Run the phases in order — each phase feeds the next.
This kit is the spine; the full product-on-purpose set has more skills per phase (discover-market-sizing, deliver-user-stories, measure-experiment-results) when you need depth.
Pair with the product-frameworks kit for the JTBD / Hook / CRO thinking behind the phases.

software-development.tagline: Write and change code the way a senior engineer would — test-first, patterned, and hard to regret.
software-development.when: You're building or refactoring a feature and want it done right, not just working.
example: Describe the feature; it starts test-first (tdd-workflow) — the failing test before the code.
It applies your stack's patterns (python / react / go / fastapi / django…) and api-design + system-design for the shape.
ponytail and karpathy-guidelines keep it minimal and free of the common LLM mistakes.
verification-before-completion runs the checks before it ever says 'done'.
tips: Name your stack so it pulls the right patterns.
Keep changes small — it won't claim verified without running the check.

data-analysis.tagline: Work with data and judge AI output without fooling yourself.
data-analysis.when: You're doing analytics, or measuring how good an AI/LLM pipeline actually is.
example: Start with error-analysis on real traces — categorize the failures before counting anything.
write-judge-prompt to build a binary Pass/Fail evaluator for the subjective calls.
validate-evaluator to calibrate that judge against human labels — never trust an uncalibrated one.
SQL + statistics for the actual numbers.
tips: Calibrate the judge before you believe its score.
Separate retrieval quality from answer quality.

product-management.tagline: The full PM toolkit — from a fuzzy idea to a shipped, measured feature.
product-management.when: You're planning and strategizing, not coding: PRDs, roadmaps, prioritization, go-to-market.
example: jobs-to-be-done to find the real need behind the request.
create-prd + user-stories to spec it.
prioritization-frameworks (RICE) to rank what to build.
north-star-metric + gtm-strategy to ship and measure it.
tips: Describe the situation, not the skills.
Pair with pm-methodology (the process) and product-frameworks (the thinking).

production-engineering.tagline: Design, ship, and operate production-grade systems — not just make it run on your laptop.
production-engineering.when: You're deploying, operating, or hardening real infrastructure.
example: system-design + deployment-patterns to shape it for production.
docker / kubernetes / terraform to actually ship it.
runbook + incident-response for when it breaks at 3am.
tips: For a specific prod bug, pair with the bug-fixing kit.
Write the runbook before you need it.

test-engineering.tagline: Make the tests actually catch things — unit, end-to-end, and regression.
test-engineering.when: You're writing or hardening a test suite you'll trust.
example: testing-strategy decides what to test at each level (and what not to).
Write the unit, end-to-end, and regression tests.
verification-before-completion so green means green.
tips: Test behavior, not implementation details.
A test that never fails is testing nothing.

application-security.tagline: Find and fix vulnerabilities the way an attacker would — then write code that resists them.
application-security.when: You're running an audit or pen-test, or hardening a feature before it ships.
example: bb-methodology to plan the hunt and scope it.
The hunt-* skills work each vulnerability class (xss, sqli, ssrf, idor, auth-bypass…).
vibesec to prevent them at write-time, not just find them.
A clean, reproducible report at the end.
tips: hunt-* finds them; vibesec prevents them.
Reproduce every finding before you report it.

frontend-design.tagline: Build interfaces people actually enjoy — polished, accessible, and alive.
frontend-design.when: You're working on anything users see on screen.
example: frontend-design for the structure and layout.
design-system + frontend patterns for consistency.
motion for how it feels.
fixing-accessibility so everyone can use it.
tips: Accessibility isn't optional — bake it in.
Motion with restraint; it should guide, not distract.

web-research.tagline: Dig into a topic and come back with a synthesized answer — not 40 open tabs.
web-research.when: You need to understand something you don't yet know.
example: deep-research plans the search — what to look for and why.
exa-search / x-research gather the raw material.
research-synthesis turns it into a clear answer with sources.
tips: Ask for sources so you can check the claims.
search-first before guessing from memory.

release-review.tagline: The gate before you ship — catch what a tired reviewer would miss.
release-review.when: You're right before a merge or a release.
example: code-review across dimensions (correctness, security, simplicity, tests).
security-audit + a check that tests actually cover the change.
verification-before-completion, and karpathy-guidelines for the common LLM slip-ups.
tips: Run it before you merge, not after.
One confirmed blocker beats ten vague nits.

bug-fixing.tagline: Find the root cause fast — not the symptom.
bug-fixing.when: Something's broken and you need it fixed now.
example: systematic-debugging to isolate the actual cause (reproduce first).
caveman-debug (print statements) when the trail goes cold.
error-handling to fix it properly, not just silence it.
tips: Reproduce before you fix.
Fix the cause, not the log line.

code-simplification.tagline: Cut the over-engineering — the best code is the code you didn't write.
code-simplification.when: A diff or a repo feels bloated and you want it lean.
example: ponytail-review on the diff — a ranked list of what to delete.
ponytail-audit for whole-repo bloat.
Keep the laziest working solution: stdlib before custom, one line before fifty.
tips: Eight sharp lines beat fifty clever ones.
Delete first; add back only what you miss.

rag-evaluation.tagline: Prove your RAG or search system actually works — retrieval and answer, scored separately.
rag-evaluation.when: You're measuring or improving a retrieval/RAG agent.
example: evaluate-rag scores retrieval quality and answer quality as separate concerns.
error-analysis on the failures to find the pattern.
write-judge-prompt + validate-evaluator for a judge you've actually calibrated.
tips: Never trust a judge you haven't calibrated against humans.
Bad retrieval and bad generation are different bugs — don't blend them.

content-writing.tagline: Write and edit docs and copy that sound human — not AI.
content-writing.when: You're writing docs or marketing copy, or cleaning up a draft.
example: draft-content / copywriting for the first pass.
no-ai-slop to strip the 20+ AI tells while keeping your voice.
ux-copy / brand-voice for tone; seo if it's for search.
tips: Run no-ai-slop after drafting, not instead of it.
Match the brand voice — generic copy converts no one.
